subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science — Physics Waves
subtitle: Reading practice passages about KS3 physics waves with comprehension questions.
description: A reading pack for KS3 waves. Passages cover the main ideas from the source, including wave transfer, sound, light, reflection, refraction, the electromagnetic spectrum and practical investigation skills.

data.sourcePassage: A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another. It does not transfer matter overall from the source to the receiver. In a sound wave, air particles vibrate backwards and forwards, but the same air particles do not travel all the way from a speaker to an ear. In a water surface wave, the water mainly moves up and down while the wave energy travels across the surface. Waves often begin at a source, such as a vibrating guitar string, a lamp, a radio transmitter or a stone dropped into water. A receiver or detector, such as an ear, eye, microphone, camera or aerial, receives the energy or information carried by the wave.

questions.question: What does a wave transfer?
questions.modelAnswer: A wave transfers energy from one place to another.

questions.question: Which statement best describes matter in many waves?
questions.modelAnswer: Particles usually vibrate around a position while energy travels.
options: Matter travels all the way from source to receiver.
Particles usually vibrate around a position while energy travels.
No particles can ever move in a wave.

questions.question: Why is an ear described as a receiver?
questions.modelAnswer: An ear receives sound energy and information carried by sound waves.

questions.question: Use the passage to explain why the same air particles from a speaker do not reach your ear.
questions.modelAnswer: The air particles vibrate backwards and forwards around their positions; the disturbance and energy travel onwards.

questions.question: Which pair is a source and detector pair?
questions.modelAnswer: A vibrating guitar string can be a source and an ear can be a detector.

data.sourcePassage: Mechanical waves need a material medium. A medium is the material a wave travels through, such as air, water, glass, metal or a rope. Sound is a mechanical wave because particles must vibrate to pass on the disturbance. This is why sound cannot travel through a vacuum. Electromagnetic waves do not need a material medium and can travel through a vacuum. Light from the Sun reaches Earth by travelling through space. Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all electromagnetic waves. At KS3, it is important to remember that radio waves are not sound waves, even though radios can turn radio signals into sound.

questions.question: What is a medium?
questions.modelAnswer: A medium is the material that a mechanical wave travels through.

questions.question: Why can light from the Sun reach Earth?
questions.modelAnswer: Light is electromagnetic, so it can travel through a vacuum.
options: Light can travel through a vacuum.
The Sun sends out particles of glass.

questions.question: Explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
questions.modelAnswer: Sound needs particles in a medium to vibrate, and a vacuum has no particles.

questions.question: Which list contains only electromagnetic waves?
questions.modelAnswer: Visible light, radio waves and X-rays are electromagnetic waves.

questions.question: Why is it misleading to call radio waves sound waves?
questions.modelAnswer: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves that can travel through a vacuum; sound waves are mechanical vibrations of particles.

data.sourcePassage: Sound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves. They are produced by vibrating objects such as speaker cones, guitar strings, drum skins and tuning forks. As the object vibrates, it creates compressions and rarefactions in the surrounding medium. Frequency is the number of vibrations each second and is measured in hertz. A higher frequency sound has a higher pitch. Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position. A larger amplitude sound wave usually sounds louder because it transfers more energy to the ear each second. Pitch and loudness are different properties. A loud drum can have a low pitch, and a quiet whistle can have a high pitch.

questions.question: What type of wave is sound?
questions.modelAnswer: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave.

questions.question: What does frequency affect in sound?
questions.modelAnswer: Frequency affects pitch.

questions.question: What does a larger amplitude usually make a sound?
questions.modelAnswer: A larger amplitude usually makes a sound louder.

questions.question: Explain why a high-pitched sound is not always loud.
questions.modelAnswer: Pitch depends on frequency, while loudness depends mainly on amplitude, so they can change independently.

questions.question: A tuning fork makes 600 vibrations in 2 seconds. Calculate its frequency.
questions.modelAnswer: Frequency equals vibrations divided by time, so 600 divided by 2 is 300 Hz.

data.sourcePassage: Light waves are transverse electromagnetic waves. They can travel through a vacuum and usually travel in straight lines through a uniform material. We see luminous objects because they give out light. We see non-luminous objects when light from a luminous object reflects from them into our eyes. Reflection happens when waves bounce off a surface. In a plane mirror ray diagram, angles are measured from the normal, an imaginary line at 90 degrees to the surface. The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Refraction is different: it is a change in direction when light crosses a boundary because its speed changes. A pencil can appear bent in water because of refraction at the water-air boundary.

questions.question: How do we see a non-luminous object?
questions.modelAnswer: Light reflects from the object into the eye.

questions.question: In reflection, where are angles measured from?
questions.modelAnswer: Angles are measured from the normal.

questions.question: State the law of reflection.
questions.modelAnswer: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

questions.question: Explain why a pencil appears bent in water.
questions.modelAnswer: Light from the underwater part changes direction as it passes from water to air, so the pencil appears displaced.

questions.question: What causes refraction?
questions.modelAnswer: Refraction is caused by a wave speed change at a boundary.
options: A speed change at a boundary

data.sourcePassage: Visible light is only one part of the electromagnetic spectrum. All electromagnetic waves are transverse, can travel through a vacuum and travel at the same speed in a vacuum. They differ in wavelength, frequency and energy. From longest wavelength and lowest frequency to shortest wavelength and highest frequency, the order is radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Different parts of the spectrum have different uses and hazards. Infrared is used in remote controls and thermal cameras. Ultraviolet can sterilise equipment but can damage skin and eyes. X-rays are useful for medical imaging, but exposure is limited because they can damage living cells.

questions.question: Which electromagnetic waves have the longest wavelength in the KS3 order?
questions.modelAnswer: Radio waves have the longest wavelength.

questions.question: Which electromagnetic waves have the highest frequency in the KS3 order?
questions.modelAnswer: Gamma rays have the highest frequency.

questions.question: Give one use of infrared radiation.
questions.modelAnswer: Infrared can be used in remote controls, thermal cameras or heaters.

questions.question: Why must ultraviolet exposure be controlled?
questions.modelAnswer: Ultraviolet can damage skin and eyes, so protection such as sunscreen, clothing or goggles may be needed.

questions.question: Which order goes from lowest frequency to highest frequency?
questions.modelAnswer: Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible is in increasing frequency order.

data.sourcePassage: Good wave investigations use clear variables and careful measurements. The independent variable is changed deliberately, and the dependent variable is measured. Control variables are kept the same to make the test fair. In a sound level and distance investigation, distance from the speaker could be the independent variable and sound level in decibels could be the dependent variable. Students should repeat readings, calculate means, check for anomalous results and use suitable graphs. Accuracy means closeness to the true value, while precision means how close repeated measurements are to each other. Safety also matters: ray boxes and bright lights should not be shone into eyes, and loud sounds should be kept at safe levels.

questions.question: What is the independent variable?
questions.modelAnswer: It is the variable deliberately changed in an investigation.

questions.question: What is the dependent variable?
questions.modelAnswer: It is the variable measured in an investigation.

questions.question: Why should control variables be kept the same?
questions.modelAnswer: They make the test fair so the independent variable is the main factor affecting the result.

questions.question: What should students do with an anomalous result?
questions.modelAnswer: They should check it and consider repeating the reading.
options: Check it and consider repeating the reading
Change all other results to match it
Use it as the only conclusion

questions.question: Give one safety precaution for wave practicals using light or sound.
questions.modelAnswer: Do not shine bright lights into eyes, keep sound levels safe, or keep cables tidy.
